sources.ref_file_title: GI14 - Distributed Point Functions and Their Applications
sources.note: EUROCRYPT 2014, pp. 640-658. The 2-server computational PIR application is the paper's flagship application of DPFs.

pages.class_justification: The PIR calls the DPF only through $\Gen$ and $\Query$/$\Answer$ evaluate it only through $\Eval$ — one fixed construction using the hypothesis as an oracle. The privacy reduction is also fixed: each server's whole view of a query is a single DPF key, so any distinguisher between queries for indices $i, i'$ is run once as an oracle and is verbatim a DPF key-hiding adversary. RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: A [[distributed-point-function|DPF]] for domain $[N]$ and range $\ZZ_2$ yields a 2-server [[multi-server-private-information-retrieval#computational-multi-server-pir|computational PIR]] for an $N$-bit database with communication proportional to the DPF key size, hence $\poly(\secpar, \log N)$: the query for index $i$ is the key pair $(k_0, k_1) \gets \Gen(1^\secpar, i, 1)$, one key per server — [[GI14 - Distributed Point Functions and Their Applications|GI14]].
pages.sketch: Server $b$ answers $a_b = \sum_{j \in [N]} D[j] \cdot \Eval(b, k_b, j)$; by DPF correctness $a_0 + a_1 = \sum_j D[j] \cdot f_{i,1}(j) = D[i]$. Each server sees only one DPF key, so query privacy against a single server reduces directly to DPF key hiding.
notes_to_keep: The construction is inherently 2-server; the conclusion node computational-multi-server-pir does not record the server count.
flags: The DPF page's Hiding property is stated as a guess-the-point game; the PIR privacy reduction needs the standard key-indistinguishability formulation (a key for $(\alpha,\beta)$ vs $(\alpha',\beta')$) — the primitive page should be fixed in the skeptical-checker lane.
Migration note about the composite OWF ⇒ DPF ⇒ PIR chain is resolved: the chain is already split (hash-function-to-prg-hill99, prg-to-dpf-gi14 exist); this page is the DPF ⇒ PIR link only.

pages.wrong_reason: The conclusion node is wrong. The migrated bullet itself says 'Computational 2-server PIR can be built from DPFs', but this edge records the base it-pir node, whose Privacy property on multi-server-private-information-retrieval.md is perfect (information-theoretic: identical query distributions). A computationally secure DPF cannot yield non-trivial information-theoretically private multi-server PIR, and GI14 claims no such thing — GI14's application is 2-server computational PIR. The correct edge already exists as red-dpf-to-computational-multi-server-pir-gi14 (content/Reductions/dpf-to-computational-multi-server-pir-gi14.md); this page is a mis-scoped duplicate and should be retired or merged into it.
flags: Duplicate of dpf-to-computational-multi-server-pir-gi14 with the conclusion collapsed to the wrong (information-theoretic) node.

sources.authors: Elette Boyle, Geoffroy Couteau, Niv Gilboa, Yuval Ishai
sources.note: cryptobib: CCS:BCGI18; full version eprint 2019/273. Formalizes multi-point FSS (MPFSS) and constructs it from DPFs via combinatorial batch codes, beating the naive t-fold blowup.

pages.class_justification: The combined $\Gen$ runs the underlying DPF's $\Gen$ once per point and the combined $\Eval$ sums the component oracle calls — one fixed construction using the DPF only as an oracle. The security proof is a fixed hybrid over the $t$ instances embedding a key-hiding challenge in one instance and running any distinguisher as an oracle.
pages.statement: A multi-point function taking value $\beta_i$ at each of $t$ distinct points $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_t$ is the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{t} f_{\alpha_i, \beta_i}$ of point functions, so sharing each summand with an independent [[distributed-point-function|DPF]] and summing the component shares in $\Eval$ gives a [[distributed-point-function#multi-point-functions|multi-point FSS]] with keys $t$ times the DPF key size — folklore.
pages.sketch: Correctness is additivity of the shares; hiding is a hybrid over the $t$ instances, replacing one key at a time, so any distinguisher yields a DPF key-hiding adversary with a factor-$t$ loss.
pages.improvements_text: - Multi-point FSS (MPFSS) formalized, with constructions from DPFs via combinatorial batch codes that beat the naive $t$-fold key blowup — [[BCGI18 - Compressing Vector OLE|BCGI18]]
flags: Conclusion node multi-point-function-secret-sharing resolves only as a variants anchor (#multi-point-functions) on distributed-point-function.md; no standalone page exists.

The migration note distinguishing the naive t-fold construction from efficient batch-code MPFSS is now resolved: the folklore statement records the naive construction and BCGI18 is cited as the improvement.

sources.ref_file_title: Rom90 - One-way functions are necessary and sufficient for secure signatures
sources.note: STOC 1990, pp. 387-394; likely cryptobib STOC:Rompel90. The paper's main content is the sufficiency direction (OWF ⇒ DS, via UOWHFs); the necessity direction recorded by this edge is the easy one asserted by the title, and the literature standardly cites this paper (sometimes alongside IL89) for the equivalence.

pages.class_justification: One fixed construction — $f$ evaluates $\KeyGen$ on its input coins and outputs the verification key — using the scheme only as an oracle, and one fixed reduction that runs any inverter once as an oracle and outputs a signature under the recovered key. RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: Every EUF-CMA-secure [[digital-signature|DS]] scheme implies a one-way function ([[hash-function|OWF]]): $f(r) := \vk$ where $(\sk, \vk) := \KeyGen(1^\secpar; r)$ is one-way, since an inverter returns coins $r'$ whose signing key produces valid signatures under $\vk$ on any message — a forgery, without even a signing query — [[Rom90 - One-way functions are necessary and sufficient for secure signatures|Rom90]].
pages.sketch: An inverter for $f$ returns $r'$ with $\KeyGen(1^\secpar; r') = (\sk', \vk)$; by correctness $\Sign(\sk', m)$ verifies under $\vk$ for every $m$, so the inverter's success probability lower-bounds the forgery probability, which unforgeability makes negligible.
flags: The origin bullet on digital-signature.md justifies the claim with a secrecy statement ('knowing the message and signature reveals nothing useful about the key'), which is not the argument — that page's prose needs the same fix (skeptical-checker lane; matches this page's migration SUSPECTED note).

Conclusion node hash-function conflates OWF with CRHF: the statement is scoped to OWF. DS does NOT imply collision-resistant hashing (black-box separation, Simon Eurocrypt 1998) — do not let the coarse node suggest otherwise.
Converse direction OWF ⇒ DS exists as its own page (hash-function-to-ds.md), for which Rom90 is also the canonical source — kind stays implication on both.

sources.ref_file_title: EGL85 - A randomized protocol for signing contracts
sources.authors: Shimon Even, Oded Goldreich, Abraham Lempel
sources.note: CACM 28(6):637-647; earlier version at CRYPTO 1982 (cryptobib C:EveGolLem82 if present). Introduces 1-out-of-2 OT and the trapdoor-based protocol; the 'enhanced' qualifier the protocol actually needs is due to Goldreich (Foundations of Cryptography vol. 2, 2004), systematized in GR13.
Pins down which enhancements the EGL OT protocol needs (enhanced TDPs) versus NIZK (doubly enhanced).

pages.class_justification: The protocol invokes the TDP only through $\Gen$, $\Eval$, $\Invert$ and the enhanced domain sampler, plus a Goldreich-Levin hard-core predicate — one fixed construction, hypothesis used as an oracle. The sender-privacy reduction converts any receiver predicting the unchosen mask into an inverter for the enhanced TDP via the black-box GL decoder; receiver privacy is perfect. RTV04 fully-black-box shape, as the page already recorded.
pages.statement: An [[trapdoor-permutation#enhanced-trapdoor-permutations|enhanced trapdoor permutation]] yields 1-out-of-2 [[oblivious-transfer|OT]] secure against semi-honest parties. In the EGL protocol the sender samples $(f, \td) \gets \Gen(1^\secpar)$ and sends $f$; the receiver with choice bit $c$ replies with $(y_0, y_1)$, where $y_c = \Eval(f, x_c)$ for random $x_c$ and $y_{1-c}$ is sampled obliviously from the domain; the sender returns each message masked by a hard-core predicate of $\Invert(\td, y_b)$ — [[EGL85 - A randomized protocol for signing contracts|EGL85]]. Enhanced one-wayness — $f$ remains hard to invert on an obliviously sampled image even given the sampling coins — is exactly what keeps the unchosen message hidden from the receiver — [[GR13 - Enhancements of Trapdoor Permutations|GR13]].
pages.sketch: Receiver privacy: $(y_0, y_1)$ are two uniform domain elements regardless of $c$. Sender privacy: a receiver predicting the unchosen message's mask predicts a hard-core bit of $f^{-1}(y_{1-c})$ given $y_{1-c}$'s sampling coins; the Goldreich-Levin decoder turns this into an inverter contradicting enhanced one-wayness.
pages.improvements_text: - Systematic treatment of the enhancement axis: enhanced TDPs suffice for EGL oblivious transfer, while NIZK needs doubly enhanced TDPs; intermediate notions separated — [[GR13 - Enhancements of Trapdoor Permutations|GR13]]
flags: MISATTRIBUTED SOURCE: GKM+00 is the PKE-vs-OT black-box separation paper and only cites this construction as background; the construction is EGL85 with Goldreich's enhancement (systematized by GR13). The frontmatter source and the slug suffix -gkm-00 should move to EGL85 (rename via scripts/rename-slugs.mjs or leave the slug and fix source; verifier's call).
Statement scoped to semi-honest security; malicious security follows via the GMW compiler — standard.

The variant blurb on trapdoor-permutation.md misstates the enhancement ('a random element $y = \Eval(f, x)$ sampled using $r$') — $y$ is sampled directly from the domain using coins $r$, and hardness is inverting $y$ given $r$; fix on the primitive page.
The page's Notes contain a migration serialization artifact: 'Citations disagree across pages: [object Object]'.

sources.ref_file_title: Wee22 - Optimal Broadcast Encryption and CP-ABE from Evasive Lattice Assumptions
sources.note: EUROCRYPT 2022 Part II, pp. 217-241; eprint 2023/906. The CP-ABE theorem assumes evasive LWE AND tensor LWE (both introduced there), plus LWE; security proven is selective.

pages.model_justification: Standard-model construction; evasive LWE and tensor LWE are (non-standard) assumptions, not idealized models.
pages.statement: [[learning-with-errors#evasive-lwe|Evasive LWE]], together with the tensor LWE assumption introduced in the same work (and [[learning-with-errors|LWE]]), yields ciphertext-policy [[attribute-based-encryption|ABE]] for circuits of a-priori bounded polynomial depth with parameter sizes independent of the circuit size; security is selective — [[Wee22 - Optimal Broadcast Encryption and CP-ABE from Evasive Lattice Assumptions|Wee22]].
flags: MISSING HYPOTHESIS: Wee22's CP-ABE theorem assumes evasive LWE AND tensor LWE; the page's hypothesis set lists only evasive-lwe. No tensor-LWE node exists in the wiki — either add one (e.g. as a variant on learning-with-errors) and add it to the hyperedge, or keep the extra assumption explicit in the statement as written here.

Evasive LWE has public-coin/private-coin variants and later counterexamples for some variants — BUW24 and AMYY25 (both already wiki refs; barrier pages no-evasive-lwe-to-evasive-lwe-buw24 and -buw24-2 exist). Worth a Notes pointer from this page.

Class left unstated: the security proof invokes evasive LWE (itself an implication between distributions quantified over samplers) in a non-standard shape; no source classifies the reduction in RTV04 terms.

sources.ref_file_title: Wee22 - Optimal Broadcast Encryption and CP-ABE from Evasive Lattice Assumptions
sources.note: EUROCRYPT 2022 Part II, pp. 217-241; eprint 2023/906. The BE result needs evasive LWE (with LWE), not tensor LWE; the first candidate optimal BE that is plausibly post-quantum secure.

pages.model_justification: Standard-model construction; evasive LWE is a (non-standard) assumption, not an idealized model.
pages.statement: [[learning-with-errors#evasive-lwe|Evasive LWE]] (together with [[learning-with-errors|LWE]]) yields optimal [[broadcast-encryption|BE]]: a broadcast encryption scheme for $N$ users in which public key, secret keys, and ciphertext overhead are all of size $\poly(\secpar, \log N)$, proven selectively secure — [[Wee22 - Optimal Broadcast Encryption and CP-ABE from Evasive Lattice Assumptions|Wee22]]. This is the first candidate optimal broadcast encryption that is plausibly post-quantum secure.
flags: The migrated 'optimal' qualifier is now made precise: parameter size poly(secpar, log N).

Unlike the sibling ABE edge, the BE theorem does not need tensor LWE; LWE is used alongside evasive LWE to establish the precondition distribution's pseudorandomness — arguably a second hypothesis on the hyperedge (the evasive-lwe node is a variant anchor of the lwe page).
Evasive LWE has public-coin/private-coin variants and later counterexamples for some variants (BUW24, AMYY25; barrier pages exist). Worth a Notes pointer.
Class left unstated: no source classifies the reduction in RTV04 terms.

pages.wrong_reason: Inverted, as both the page's own SUSPECTED notes and .reductions/suspected-errors.json record. Given the factorization of $n$ one computes $\varphi(n)$ and decides $n$-th residuosity in $\ZZ_{n^2}^*$ by testing $z^{\varphi(n)} \bmod n^2$, so a factoring algorithm breaks DCR; hence DCR hardness implies factoring hardness — DCR is the stronger assumption. The converse (factoring hard ⇒ DCR hard) is open, and Pai99 proves no such implication (Pai99 only notes the scheme falls to factoring). Correct edge: DCR ⇒ FAC (folklore; a dcr-to-fac page does not yet exist in content/Reductions/).
flags: The same inverted bullet appears on decisional-composite-residuosity.md:30 and factoring.md:31 and must be fixed there too; decisional-composite-residuosity.md:31 additionally inverts which direction is open (suspected-errors entries cover both).
When creating the corrected dcr-to-fac edge, its class is fully-black-box (the trivial reduction runs a factoring oracle once and then decides residuosity).

sources.ref_file_title: GMR88 - A Digital Signature Scheme Secure Against Adaptive Chosen-Message Attacks
sources.authors: Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali, Ronald L. Rivest
sources.note: Defines EUF-CMA and constructs the first signature scheme meeting it, generically from claw-free trapdoor permutation pairs, with a factoring-based instantiation.

pages.class_justification: One fixed (stateful, tree-based) construction generic over claw-free trapdoor permutation pairs, used only as oracles; one fixed security reduction that runs any forger as an oracle and converts its forgery into a claw, which for the factoring-based pair (built from squaring modulo $N$) yields the factorization of the challenge modulus. RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: If [[factoring|FAC]] is hard, EUF-CMA-secure [[digital-signature|DS]] schemes exist: GMR construct a stateful signature scheme secure against existential forgery under adaptive chosen-message attack from any claw-free pair of trapdoor permutations, and instantiate claw-free pairs under the intractability of factoring — [[GMR88 - A Digital Signature Scheme Secure Against Adaptive Chosen-Message Attacks|GMR88]].
pages.sketch: Signing authenticates the message down an authentication tree using inverses of the claw-free pair $(f_0, f_1)$; the reduction turns any forgery into a claw $(x_0, x_1)$ with $f_0(x_0) = f_1(x_1)$, and a claw for the squaring-based pair reveals the factors of the modulus.
flags: The migration note is right that 'based on factoring' hides the intermediate object: the generic hypothesis is a claw-free trapdoor permutation pair; the statement now names it. If the wiki ever adds a claw-free-permutation node, this edge should be split into FAC ⇒ claw-free pair ⇒ DS.
The origin bullet on digital-signature.md lacks a wikilink to factoring — fix when applying.

pages.wrong_reason: Inverted, as the page's own SUSPECTED notes and .reductions/suspected-errors.json record (high confidence there too). Knowing $p$ and $q$ lets one compute Legendre symbols mod $p$ and $q$ and thereby decide quadratic residuosity mod $N = pq$, so a factoring algorithm breaks QR; hence QR hardness implies factoring hardness — QR is the stronger assumption. Whether factoring hardness implies QR hardness is a long-standing open question, and GM84 makes no such claim (GM84 introduce the QR assumption and prove semantic security of their scheme under it). The bullet's own justification ('knowing $p$ and $q$ allows computing the Legendre symbols') proves the opposite direction of the one asserted. Correct edge: QR ⇒ FAC (folklore; a qr-to-fac page does not yet exist in content/Reductions/).
flags: The same inverted bullet appears on factoring.md:30 and quadratic-residuosity.md (Known Results) and must be fixed there; the Attacks section of quadratic-residuosity.md already states the correct direction and contradicts it.
When creating the corrected qr-to-fac edge, its class is fully-black-box (the trivial reduction runs a factoring oracle once, then computes Legendre symbols).
